Migration plan

Where each of the 473 entities in html-spec's own OpenSpec project goes when the repository becomes an html-spec project (286 carried, 121 converted, 1 dropped, 65 folded), across 36 archived changes, 13 accepted specifications, and the project's own two files. This is the second attempt, written from main at 139b206. It stopped for review before anything was staged, because reading it is the only review that catches a mechanical conversion, and it was reviewed on 2026-10-13. What the second review decided comes first, then the decisions the first review settled, as amended.

The second attempt

The first attempt reviewed this plan on 2026-09-29, then staged and checked the whole project from 6a591bd: 109 documents and 301 of 301 entities, with promotion's check passing. It stopped before promotion on 2026-09-30, so that the destination could first gain the vocabulary the migration had been working around. Ten changes gave it that vocabulary (0.19.0 to 0.28.0). A formatter fix (0.28.1) and the request-verb spellings (0.29.0) followed. This plan is the second attempt, written from main at 139b206. Nothing has been staged, and the repository is untouched.

Requirement derivations, and the identifiers they resolve to 308, 137 353, 149
Scenario identifiers qualified under decision 2 7 27
Greatest recorded version 0.18.0 0.29.0
Dispositions 169 carried, 85 converted, 46 folded, 1 dropped 286 carried, 121 converted, 65 folded, 1 dropped

What carried over. None of the 24 older archives has changed since 6a591bd, so their readers' reports carry over unchanged. So do the notes on the six accepted specifications whose text is unchanged. Sixteen new readers read the twelve new archives and the seven changed specifications. The five decisions and eight conventions stand as reviewed, with dated amendments where the second attempt revised them. The replay of every delta in archive order reproduces all 13 accepted specifications at 139b206 exactly, and agrees with the accepted specifications at every archival commit. So no new exception to a delta's merge is needed. Every open question a first-attempt or second-attempt reader recorded was then classified as of 139b206. Each task below shows a question as Open only where nothing has settled it. A settled one says what settled it and keeps the question beside it.

What the destination now maps. Each distinction below was recorded as a workaround in the first attempt, because the destination had no value for it. Each now has one, and project-migration's "A source distinction the destination cannot express is recorded as open, not mapped to the nearest state" requires the migration to map it. The second column's counts are what the new readers found in the twelve new archives. The third is what the first attempt worked around in the older ones, as openspec/changes/archive/2026-10-08-migrate-into-the-extended-vocabulary/evidence/the-measurement-2026-09-30.md records it. Drafting finds each instance. These counts are what this review can expect.

The new readers also found 70 records of a check that reached the whole of what it names. Each becomes a passed verification citing its record (convention 6), as the second review's question 4 limits it. No new archive gives a risk its own heading, so their risks stay in prose, and no new archive strikes a task.

What staging will do differently. A fresh init at 0.29.0, so every document links the stylesheet the program now writes and the store holds nothing a document does not name. The first attempt's staged tree is not reused. Every document is drafted again under the revised brief, one drafter per packet, for 49 packets: 13 accepted specifications and 36 changes. The first attempt's drafts predate the vocabulary, and the six packets its proof re-drafted in the new vocabulary survived only in a scratch directory that no longer exists. The formatter fault the first attempt's drafters worked around, which rewrote a quoted href=" in prose, was fixed by 2026-10-09-fill-only-the-references-a-document-loads, so that workaround goes.

What the second review decided

Eight questions the second attempt could not settle by a requirement, a reviewed decision, or a convention. Each gathers what several readers raised on their own. Each was put to review on 2026-10-13 with the coordinator's recommendation, and review adopted every recommendation the same day. The question is kept beside the answer, as the first review's are.

  1. Scenario identifiers across documents. Decision 2, as amended on 2026-10-08, makes a scenario a change carries forward take its accepted counterpart's identifier. In 2026-10-04-resolve-a-reference-across-its-change that cannot hold. Its one specification carries forward both "Reference to a removed requirement" scenarios, from document-schema and from document-validation, so each must be qualified there to stay unique. Each accepted counterpart is alone in its accepted specification and keeps the unqualified identifier. Eleven scenarios share a heading with another in some document. Under the rule as it stands, nine of them carry a different identifier in different documents.

    Decided, as recommended: One identifier per scenario, in every document that holds it. A scenario that shares a heading with another scenario in any destination document is qualified in every document that holds it, from its requirement's identifier and its own heading. That is the scenario's counterpart to "one obligation, one identifier". It removes the conflict, and it keeps a scenario findable by one name across the archive and the accepted contract. It changes the identifier the first review settled for these eleven scenarios in three accepted specifications (artifact-kinds, document-schema, document-validation) and five changes. Nothing is staged yet, so the change costs nothing. The alternative keeps decision 2 local and qualifies an accepted counterpart only where a change must qualify a scenario it carries forward. Today that touches only the resolve-a-reference pair, and it leaves the other differences between documents in place.

  2. Design decisions the status vocabulary does not fit. A decision unit declares proposed, accepted, or superseded (document-schema's "A decision records its outcome and rationale"). Readers met five kinds of decision that fit none of these cleanly. Some designs state no status at all. Some decisions read "Confirm at review" and are settled only in a task's record. Some were built otherwise than written, and the author never corrected them: request-verb decisions 4 and 5, see-a-modification decisions 1, 6, and 7, and fill-only decision 3, among others. Some a later change reversed, as distinguish-command-names-from-skill-names reversed conform's decision 1, and as record-a-renamed-requirement reversed three of migrate-an-openspec-project's. And some narrate their own earlier form, or are "Rejected:" sections.

    Decided, as recommended: Keep the brief's shape test, and carry the rest as written with notes. A decision becomes a unit only where the drafting brief's shape test holds. Such a unit is accepted, because its change was archived. That holds whether or not the source states a status, and for a decision whose own text defers it, with a note naming the task record that settled it. A decision built otherwise, or reversed later, stays accepted as written. A migration note says what was built, or which later change reversed it, and links that record (convention 2). superseded is not used: its successor would sit in another change, which a change's documents cannot reach (document-schema's "Cross-references address units by identifier"). "Rejected:" sections, and decisions that narrate their own history, stay prose under their own headings. A decision built otherwise is listed below as a distinction the destination cannot express.

  3. When a task owes a deviation. project-migration's "A source task is carried in the state its record supports" asks for a deviation where a ticked task's record says the work was done otherwise than its words, only in part, or beyond them, and sets no floor. Readers disagreed nine times in five reports. One mapped a Python stage run outside nix develop as a deviation, and another left the same fact unmapped. A third case recurs too: an earlier task's evidence file records checks that belong to a later task's fix.

    Decided, as recommended: A deviation states a difference in the result. It is owed where the record says something was built, decided, or recorded otherwise than the task's words, only in part, or beyond them. How the work was carried out is not one, such as which shell ran it, or an extra check along the way. Where the record states it, a migration note may carry it. Work an earlier task's evidence records for a later task belongs to the later task. The packets for the 24 older archives will carry the 76 rows of 2026-10-08-record-a-task-done-differently/evidence/the-measurement-2026-09-30.md, and the checker will report a draft that disagrees with them.

  4. Test names as evidence. Several records give a passing test only by a name that spells a scenario's heading, such as a_struck_through_phrase_reports_nothing, with no assertion shown. Several tasks mention such a test.

    Decided, as recommended: A test name is not the author's words naming a scenario, so a task that mentions one carries no data-refs for it. A record that gives only a test's name and its passing becomes a verification only where the drafter reads the test at the record's commit and finds that it checks the scenario's condition and outcome. That is passed, or partial where it checks part. Otherwise no verification is written.

  5. A verification of a requirement the change does not state. record-a-partial-verification's mutation record checks runbook-execution's "A run's conformance to its runbook's contract is reported and never gated", which that change does not state.

    Decided, as recommended: None is written. A change's specification verifies the requirements it states. The check stays in the change's evidence and the task that cites it.

  6. Links the source did not write. Readers asked about links the author never wrote: forward links from an archived change to a later change that corrected or reversed it, links from an uncited figure to another change's evidence, links from an accepted specification's quoted heading to the requirement it quotes, and links from a claim in an accepted specification to an archived change's evidence.

    Decided, as recommended: Add none. A migrated document gains a link only where a convention or a requirement asks for it. Convention 3 gives a cited source path a link to its migrated counterpart and gives a unit the author names data-refs. "Evidence crosses unchanged" links a change's documents to that change's own evidence. A migration note links the record it names. A quoted heading in an accepted specification stays text. A later change whose subject is cross-linking can add the rest.

  7. Drafting conventions the first attempt used without review. The drafting brief carries working rules the first attempt's accepted drafts followed. The plan never put them to review.

    Decided, as recommended: Adopt them as conventions 9 to 12. (9) A task's heading is its source number and its first sentence as written, and the rest of its line is a paragraph beneath. (10) A source's own title line is not carried into the body, and the masthead's heading replaces it. The heading is the source's title where it is a real one, such as "Sync: the operation archival tells you to run". It is the change's name in words where the title is only # Design, # Tasks, or # Proposal, and the capability's name for an accepted specification, whose # <capability> Specification line states nothing more. (11) The drafters of 2026-08-10-html-spec and 2026-08-13-content-address-runtime-assets are told that evidence/the-collapse-produced-2026-09-09.html is the failure to avoid, and that evidence/a-migrated-design-2026-09-09.html is a reviewed reading they may consult and must not copy. Both stay byte-identical evidence. (12) No figure is drawn across several requirements. A figure sits beside the statements of one requirement (convention 5).

  8. Quoted markup. The twelve new archives' documents, and four accepted specifications, are about html-spec's own vocabulary, and quote ins, del, and unit markup in prose. Validation rejects most live change markup. It accepts the marks inside a requirement or scenario marked modified, and in free prose a live unit is read into the model. In those places only a reader would see a quotation turned live.

    Decided, as recommended: Add a mechanical check. Before drafting, the checker gains a rule. Every source code span that quotes markup must appear in the draft as text, and the checker reports one that does not. Inside a modified unit, the marks check already compares the unit with the replay's text in both directions, which catches a quotation turned into a mark.

What was decided

Five questions where the contract is silent, the source holds something the destination cannot express, or the product disagrees with its contract. The plan stopped on them before anything was staged, and each was answered in review on 2026-09-29. The question is kept beside the answer.

  1. Creation dates. Fifteen changes record in .openspec.yaml the date the change was started, for example migrate-an-openspec-project, created 2026-08-24 and archived 2026-09-11. The destination has no field for a creation date. The 2026-09-09 plan dropped them, saying the archive directory's name already records the date. That was wrong: the name records the archive date. The plan proposed dropping the files and recording each date in its task. The alternative was to carry each file byte-identical into its change's evidence/, which stretches artifact-kinds' definition of evidence, "a record of why the change has the shape it does", to cover a configuration file.

    Decided: Carry each one. Every .openspec.yaml crosses byte-identical to evidence/.openspec.yaml in its change. The three that also name a predecessor are stated again as a FOLLOWS file, which is the declaration the program reads. The name inside evidence/ is the migration's choice, since the contract is silent on it, and it keeps the source's.

    Amended on 2026-10-08, by migrate-into-the-extended-vocabulary, for the plan's next review: The carrying stands, and its reason changes. The question said the destination has no field for a creation date, as though a change still to come would add one. On 2026-10-01 the project decided not to record a creation date, because no command depends on one, and withdrew the change that would have added it. So the date is neither mapped nor an open question, and it crosses only inside the carried file, under project-migration's "A source change's own configuration is surveyed, and its predecessor becomes its declaration". Each FOLLOWS is now written from the survey's payload, which reports every change's configuration, rather than from a second reading of the file, and no entity's reason restates its date.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: The archive has grown since the question was put. The survey at 139b206 reports 27 change configurations, 9 of which state a predecessor, against 15 and 3. Each is carried by the same rule.

  2. Scenario identifiers that collide. Three pairs of scenarios share a heading inside one destination document. Two arise in collapsed specifications (2026-08-10-html-spec: "Reference to a removed requirement"; 2026-08-14-separate-artifact-kinds: "A tasks document carrying other units"), and one in the accepted toolchain-packaging ("An invalid specification", under two requirements). project-migration's identifier requirement governs requirement identifiers only, and forbids resolving a collision by suffixing. On scenarios the contract is silent.

    Decided: As proposed. A scenario's identifier is scenario- plus its heading, derived the way a requirement's is. Only where two scenarios in one document share a heading is each derived from its requirement's heading followed by its own, and each of those six is recorded as a scenario: note on the task that stated it. None of the six requirements was renamed, so its heading and its identifier agree. The same scenario keeps the unqualified identifier in any document where it has no twin. The source text is not changed, and the rule is the migration's, not the contract's.

    Amended on 2026-10-08, by migrate-into-the-extended-vocabulary, for the plan's next review: A scenario a change carries forward, alters, or withdraws takes the identifier its accepted counterpart carries, as artifact-kinds' "A change's specification states a modified requirement whole" requires: the scenario the accepted specification holds under the same requirement with the same heading. So a qualified identifier follows the scenario into a change's specification even where it has no twin there. This changes one scenario, "An invalid specification", which 2026-09-26-record-a-renamed-requirement carries forward unchanged: it now carries scenario-the-command-surface-reports-whether-a-change-reached-the-accepted-contract-an-invalid-specification, and its delta's task records it with a scenario: note. A scenario a change adds is unaffected.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: The archive the rule applies to has grown. Twelve changes archived since bring five more shared headings, so eight clash in all. The new ones are "An invalid specification" in 2026-10-02-see-a-modification-the-merge-did-not-take, and under a third requirement in the accepted toolchain-packaging; "Reference to a removed requirement" in 2026-10-04-resolve-a-reference-across-its-change, the pair 2026-08-10-html-spec already had; "A change with a task done differently" in 2026-10-08-record-a-task-done-differently and the accepted toolchain-packaging; and "The history is read from the archive" in the accepted artifact-kinds. The resolve-a-reference pair broke the rule as amended, because its accepted counterparts were unqualified, and nine scenarios carried different identifiers in different documents. The second review settled it on 2026-10-13 (its question 1). A scenario that shares a heading with another scenario in any document is qualified in every document that holds it, from its requirement's identifier and its own heading. So one scenario holds one identifier everywhere. 11 scenarios are qualified, and the plan records each on every task whose document holds it, 27 scenario: notes in all. This replaces the answer's "keeps the unqualified identifier in any document where it has no twin".

  3. project-bootstrap's purpose. Its ## Purpose is the placeholder openspec archive writes ("TBD - created by archiving change project-bootstrap-cli. Update Purpose after archive."). A migrated accepted specification opens with a summary a consumer reads. The alternative carries the placeholder, which the destination's own review rules would flag as unwritten prose.

    Decided: Write one. The summary is written from the specification's own requirements, says nothing they do not, and is marked in the document as text the source did not contain.

  4. Where this plan goes, and what the next change must do. The plan records how the project arrived, and it is not a surveyed entity. It was proposed as evidence of the first change made in html-spec form. That change points scripts/check-release, the self-runbooks stages, and the migration tests at htmlspec/, and removes openspec/. The release runbook sits at runbooks/release/, outside openspec/, so the survey does not list it, and runbook-authority and project-bootstrap put a project's runbooks under htmlspec/runbooks/. Its two documents link the stylesheet revisions e4f5de7… and 0350261…, which the repository's own assets/ retains and a store made by init does not. Otherwise the runbook's bytes change and its version must advance at the next archival, because the runbooks.json inventories fingerprint it.

    Decided: As proposed, and that change moves the runbook too. It moves runbooks/release/ to htmlspec/runbooks/release/ byte-identical, with the two retained stylesheet revisions kept in htmlspec/assets/, so the runbook's version stays 0.1.0. Promotion itself leaves openspec/ and runbooks/ in place, as project-migration's "The source project survives migration" requires.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: Re-checked at 139b206. The runbook's two documents still link e4f5de7… and 0350261…, the repository's assets/ still holds both, and a store made by this program's init still holds neither: it writes the stylesheet revisions 03627137… and 04ac9a24…. scripts/check-release still reads openspec/. Nothing in the answer changes. One consequence the plan had not stated: until promotion, htmlspec archive and htmlspec sync cannot run on this repository, which is why the twelve changes since were archived through OpenSpec (2026-09-06-distinguish-a-requirement-from-an-example, task 6.4, assigned the record to the migration). Promotion is what closes that gap.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: The plan was promoted on 2026-10-13, as commit 071d67a (pull request #55). The promotion exposed a defect: new document found its project from the working directory, so with this repository now a project, scripts/check failed. The contributor chose to fix it first, as an html-spec change. So the first change made in html-spec form is resolve-a-new-documents-project-from-its-destination (release 0.29.1, pull request #56), and the follow-on change this decision describes becomes the second. What the follow-on change does is unchanged, and this plan is still its evidence.

  5. Where a change built something other than it stated. project-migration's "A change's delta specifications collapse into that change's one specification" says the implemented result is what the migrated specification records. The readers found such differences in about half the changes, listed under each change below. Most are deliberate, such as review rounds that changed run after the delta was written. Two are defects still in the product, confirmed by reading the code. archive is dispatched without --store, so it acts on the local project, which the flag's help says never happens. And archive --check never tests whether the archive target exists, because that test is in the path --check skips.

    Decided: As proposed. An archived change's specification records what that change built, with a note naming each deviation. An accepted specification is converted as the contract states it today. The two defects are fixed in a change of their own and are not written into the contract.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: Both defects are still in the product at 139b206, confirmed by reading the code. archive is still dispatched without the global --store (crates/htmlspec-cli/src/main.rs), whose help still says it never falls back to the project you are standing in. The collision test is still only in perform (crates/htmlspec-cli/src/commands.rs), which --check returns before. No change since has fixed either, so the answer stands. The twelve changes archived since are read under the same rule. Reading found three more places where the product does not do what an accepted specification says, each confirmed at 139b206 and listed under "Found while reading". They are handled the same way: the accepted specification is converted as it states the contract, and the product is a matter for a change of its own.

How the documents will be written

Conventions every drafter follows, each answering something several readers raised independently. The first eight were put in the same review as the decisions above, before any document was drafted, and accepted as written. The second review adopted conventions 9 to 12 on 2026-10-13 (its question 7).

  1. Task and decision numbers stay visible. Carried evidence cites work by number, such as "task 5.6" and "decision 3", and cannot be edited. So each migrated task's heading keeps its source number, and so does each design decision.

  2. Records are carried as written, and so is disagreement with them. A task marked done that nothing records happening, done differently, or struck through keeps its source state. A note names the disagreement and links the evidence. A figure later corrected, such as 31 diagnostics that were really 36, stays as the author wrote it, with a link to the correction. Nothing is silently fixed, because the argument was made with the figure the author had.

    Amended on 2026-10-08, by migrate-into-the-extended-vocabulary, for the plan's next review: A task the source strikes through, or marks [~], is dropped with the source's reason, whichever box is ticked, because the source states that the work was given up. A task done otherwise than its words say is done, and states what was done in a deviation paragraph rather than a note: in the author's words where the task's text carries the account, and otherwise saying what was done and where that is shown. A task done that nothing records stays done, with its note. The rule for tasks and this convention disagreed about a task ticked and struck through; the rule for tasks wins (project-migration's "A source task is carried in the state its record supports").

  3. Source paths stay as text, and links go to the migrated counterpart. Prose citing openspec/specs/…/spec.md:36 or a pre-archive path keeps the text. Where the target has a migrated counterpart, such as a requirement or a document, the citation also links there. Paths inside evidence are untouched.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: Where a task or a decision names a requirement or a scenario by its heading, and the document reaches that unit, it also carries the unit's identifier in data-refs, beside the link, which stays (project-migration's "A unit the author's words name is referenced wherever the migrated project resolves it"). A unit only another change declares, or one the place resolving it marks removed, keeps the link alone. The drafting brief has said so since 2026-10-08, and this convention had not.

  4. Per-scenario change states come from the archive itself. A MODIFIED delta restates a whole requirement and cannot say which scenarios are new, and in the destination a scenario with no state reads as unchanged. So each modified requirement is compared with its previous statement in the archive, the earlier change's delta, replayed in archive order, and its scenarios and paragraphs are marked added or modified accordingly. The source archive is the evidence, not git history. The comparison is mechanical and is recorded per change.

    Amended on 2026-10-08, by migrate-into-the-extended-vocabulary, for the plan's next review: Where the replay and the history differ, the accepted specification at the commit that applied the change's contract decides, as it did for the two scenarios separate-artifact-kinds' merge kept. replay_vs_history.py compares the replay with every archival commit and finds no other difference. The previous text of each modified requirement and scenario now goes to the drafter in the packet, who marks the words the change added and deleted with ins and del (project-migration's "A change's delta specifications collapse into that change's one specification").

  5. A normative list keeps projecting. The projection takes a requirement's statements from its paragraphs only. So each item of a normative list or table cell holds its text in a <p>. A Mermaid flow added for a sequence, such as artifact-kinds' archival order and its gate, sits beside the statements and never replaces them. A diagram states nothing the model can read.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: The convention applies to a list or a table that is itself the statement, as a source list is. A table a drafter adds beside the statements, to show what they already say, holds no <p> in its cells, just as a diagram sits beside them. toolchain-packaging's "The command surface reports whether a change reached the accepted contract" compares a requirement's statements as an ordered list of paragraphs. So a <p> in such a table would put each statement into the model twice, and would change what the next change that restates the requirement is compared against. Each source paragraph stays one <p>.

  6. Evidence and verification units only where a record exists. project-migration forbids manufacturing a unit kind the source has no record of. A verification unit is written only where an evidence file records the outcome of checking that requirement or scenario, and it cites the file. Everywhere else the omission is recorded, and review/unverified-requirement warnings remain as the honest state.

    Amended on 2026-10-13, for the second attempt, which re-surveyed main at 139b206: A record that reached part of a requirement or scenario and not the rest is a verification too, with outcome partial and one unchecked paragraph for each part it did not reach, in the requirement's or scenario's words (project-migration's "A check that reached part of what it names is carried as a partial verification"). The first attempt's review removed two verifications for being partial, and staged two more as passed. Each is now partial. A check whose condition, subject, or trigger differs from the scenario's still yields no verification.

  7. Removed requirements keep their reasons. A requirement under ## REMOVED Requirements is migrated with data-change="removed". Its Reason and Migration paragraphs, which have no field, become note paragraphs, so the model keeps them. A scenario withdrawn without a delta, as in distinguish-command-names-from-skill-names, is an open question for its change.

    Amended on 2026-10-08, by migrate-into-the-extended-vocabulary, for the plan's next review: A scenario a MODIFIED block left out is no longer an open question. It is completed from the source's own merge: unchanged, with its text, where the accepted specification at the archival commit still held it, and removed, with the text it held before, where it did not. distinguish-command-names-from-skill-names' "One identity per workflow" is the second case. Only an omission the history cannot settle goes to review (project-migration's "A change's delta specifications collapse into that change's one specification").

  8. The hand-converted documents cross as they are today. The four documents/*.html files were edited after archival. They are carried with their current bytes, the ones in the repository at promotion, into evidence/documents/. Content that only they hold, such as separate-artifact-kinds' dogfooding findings, is linked from that change's converted documents.

  9. A task's heading is its number and first sentence. Each checkbox line becomes a task whose heading is its source number and its first sentence as written, and the rest of the line is a paragraph beneath. Nothing is composed. The first attempt's accepted drafts followed this without review.

  10. A source's title line gives way to the masthead. A source's own title line is not carried into the body, and the masthead's heading replaces it. The heading is the source's title where it is a real one, such as "Sync: the operation archival tells you to run". It is the change's name in words where the title is only # Design, # Tasks, or # Proposal, and the capability's name for an accepted specification, whose # <capability> Specification line states nothing more.

  11. Two hand-made migrations in evidence are a warning and a reading. The drafters of 2026-08-10-html-spec and 2026-08-13-content-address-runtime-assets are told that 2026-09-11-migrate-an-openspec-project/evidence/the-collapse-produced-2026-09-09.html passed every check and is the failure to avoid, and that evidence/a-migrated-design-2026-09-09.html is a reviewed reading they may consult and must not copy. Both stay byte-identical evidence.

  12. No figure spans requirements. A figure the drafter adds sits beside the statements of one requirement (convention 5). None is drawn across several, such as toolchain-packaging's archival modes, because no requirement places one there.

The rules every task below applies

Dispositions are one of four words. Converted becomes a document, folded becomes part of another artifact, carried crosses byte for byte, and dropped does not cross. A folded or dropped task states why.

Source Disposition Destination What decides it
specs/<cap>/spec.md (accepted) converted htmlspec/specs/<cap>/spec.html Silent on the layout beneath htmlspec/specs/, so the source's nested path is preserved.
proposal.md, design.md, tasks.md converted htmlspec/changes/archive/<dir>/<name>.html project-migration's "Conversion of a document's meaning is agent-driven".
Delta specs/<cap>/spec.md folded the change's one specification.html project-migration's "A change's delta specifications collapse into that change's one specification".
VERSION carried same relative path project-migration's "Migrated archives carry their versions where the archival gate reads them".
evidence/**, runbooks.json carried same relative path project-migration's "Evidence crosses unchanged". A runbook inventory is carried because project-bootstrap's "The release suite checks published runbook version history" reads it.
documents/*.html carried evidence/documents/<name>.html project-migration's "A source entity already in the destination format is not assumed usable", with artifact-kinds' evidence requirement. The directory name is the migration's choice.
.openspec.yaml carried evidence/.openspec.yaml in its change, and a FOLLOWS file written from its follows: where the survey reports one project-migration's "A source change's own configuration is surveyed, and its predecessor becomes its declaration", with artifact-kinds' "A change states the change it follows". Decision 1 carries the file.
Archive directory names carried <date>-<name> unchanged toolchain-packaging's "An archived change is named for its date and refuses to collide". No version is composed into a name.

Identifiers. Each requirement's identifier is req- and its full heading, lowercased, with every other run of characters made one hyphen, derived once and recorded as a derives: line on the task for the document that stated it. There are 353 derivations, which resolve to 149 distinct identifiers with no collision. The one recorded rename chain is: "A single command exposes validate, format, and init" became "… bootstrap, and create" in project-bootstrap-cli, then "The command surface names its operations as OpenSpec names them" in finish-the-archival. Every change in it resolves to req-a-single-command-exposes-validate-format-and-init, as does the accepted specification.

The release record. Seven changes record 0.1.0. The repository's CHANGELOG.md already has a 0.1.0 entry naming all seven, and it stays where it is. spec.nix declares the greatest recorded version, 0.29.0.

The project's own files

The two files at the top of openspec/. The survey lists nothing else outside a change or an accepted specification.

  • openspec/config.yaml

    Does: Selects OpenSpec's spec-driven workflow for the whole project, and nothing else: its context, rules, and operations blocks are OpenSpec's commented-out template, so no authoring rule or project context was ever set here.

    source: openspec/config.yaml

    destination: none

    disposition: dropped

    It sets one key, schema: spec-driven, which selects OpenSpec's workflow and has no counterpart: the destination has one workflow and its declaration carries no schema choice. Its context, rules, and operations blocks are OpenSpec's commented-out examples, so they carried nothing. This is a file whose one set value has nowhere to go, not content that was lost.

  • openspec/runbook-releases.json

    Does: Marks 0.15.0 as the release from which every archive must carry a runbook inventory, so an archive before it may lack one and an archive after it that lacks one is an error rather than old history.

    source: openspec/runbook-releases.json

    destination: htmlspec/runbook-releases.json

    disposition: carried

    reason: The adoption marker naming 0.15.0 as the first release whose archives must carry a runbook inventory, as project-bootstrap's "The release suite checks published runbook version history" requires. The contract is silent on where the marker lives. The program reads it at the planning root (ProjectRoot::runbook_releases), which is where the source kept it, so the shape is preserved.

The evidence requirement (2026-09-29) sits at 2, the predecessor pair (2026-09-02) at 3 and 4, the rename (2026-09-26) at 12, the described change (2026-08-22) at 13, the whole statement (2026-10-02) at 14, and the marked modification (2026-10-07) at 15. project-bootstrap: Placeholder. `TBD - created by archiving change project-bootstrap-cli. Update Purpose after archive.` was written by `openspec archive`. None of the 8 deltas that touched this capability ever carried a `## Purpose`. From the requirements, an author-written Purpose would have to say that this capability establishes an html-spec project and keeps it coherent over time. It would name: the `htmlspec/` root with its four places (accepted specifications, active changes, archive, runbooks) around exactly one asset store; a declaration of name, version, and expected program, written in the build's own language, that at least one command depends on; resolving the project from any directory without crossing the repository boundary; installing agent instructions per selected tool, covering the whole lifecycle in order, loadable, named once per tool, carrying what the contributor typed, and confined to a marked region in shared files; a bootstrap that is repeatable without loss, names the lifecycle's entry command, and tells a cancellation from a failure. It would also have to say that the capability owns the project's version history. Archival refuses unless the declared version advances past the version the last archived change recorded, and published runbooks are held to their own version ordering, both at archival and by the release suite. That last part is three of the twelve requirements and 1,643 of the 5,969 words, so a Purpose describing bootstrapping alone would misdescribe the capability. A reader looking for the version gate would not look under this name. I have not written one. Keep source order.     Does: Makes formatting a contract rather than a style: one canonical byte form for any content, a fixed point, no churn outside the edited unit, a deterministic order for generated content, a fixed encoding and line ending, and a check that writes nothing so that CI can reject unformatted documents. Its one carve-out was added on 2026-10-09, partly because this migration's own drafters twice had a quoted `href` rewritten. It lets formatting fill an asset reference whose bytes the store lacks only where an element loads the asset, never in a hyperlink or in quoted text, and that is what lets every migrated document quote an attribute plainly.

    Format: ## Purpose: written by an author and identical to the 2026-08-10-html-spec delta's.     Format: HIGHEST RISK IN THE SLICE. Scenarios 'A word inserted into a statement' and 'A deleted word beside an inserted phrase' (source lines 409 and 413) quote a statement's HTML in their WHEN, with tags nested inside it: `<code>status</code>`, `<ins><code>sync</code>, </ins>`, `<del>and </del>`, and `<ins>and its runbooks, </ins>`. Each WHEN quotation must be a single <code> element whose whole content is escaped text (&lt;ins&gt;&lt;code&gt;sync&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;/ins&gt; and so on). Keep the leading ellipsis and the trailing spaces inside each ins and del. If the markup is left live, document-validation's 'Change markup in or around a semantic unit is rejected' rejects the accepted specification, because marks are permitted only in a modified unit of a change's specification. The projection would also drop the del's text from the WHEN entry (projection.md section 8.6.1), so the scenario would state a different condition while acting out its own rule. The THEN entries quote the resulting plain text in double quotes. Keep those as plain text.

    Format: Scenario 'Recognized unit' (line 12) quotes `<section class="requirement" id="req-theme-selection">`. Escape it inside <code>. Left live, it opens a requirement nested inside a scenario, which projection.md section 4.3 makes invalid.

    Format: Requirement 'A renamed requirement states the heading it replaced' quotes `<span class="hs-id">req-x</span>` in its last paragraph (line 97). Its scenario 'A heading that shows its identifier' quotes `The name <span class="hs-id">req-x</span>` (line 134). Escape both inside <code>. Left live, the span renders as an identifier badge, and the scenario no longer shows the markup it is about.

    Format: Attribute quotations, each to stay escaped text inside <code> and never a live attribute: `class="note"` and `class="requirement"` (scenarios of 'Semantic units are identified by class'); every `data-change="…"` value, including the invalid `pending` ('Semantic units declare a change state', and the rename requirement); `data-field="renamed-from"` (the rename requirement); `data-refs`, `href="#…"`, and `#req-x` ('Cross-references address units by identifier'); `data-field="deviation"` ('A task declares completion state'); `ins`, `del`, and `deletions` (the last list item of 'The HTML-to-model projection is published as a normative specification', and all of 'A deleted word is recorded apart from what a unit states'); `data-field="unchecked"` and `data-outcome="partial|failed|passed"` ('A partial verification states what it did not check'); `data-response` with each of its values, including the invalid `partial`, plus `data-field="mitigation"` and `data-state` ('A risk records how it was settled').

    Format: Example identifiers `req-theme-selection`, `scenario-theme-persists`, `req-does-not-exist`, `req-x`, `req-y`, and `#req-x` (scenarios of 'Cross-references address units by identifier', 'Semantic units are identified by class', and the rename requirement) stay <code> text. None of them may become a `data-refs` value or an `href="#…"` link. In an accepted specification either one would be a real reference that resolves to nothing, and the scenario 'A fragment link to a unit in another document' is about exactly that link.

    Format: Requirement 'Every semantic unit has a stable unique identifier': the mapping from unit to prefix is one sentence in the THEN of 'Prefix matches unit type'. Keep the sentence where it is.

    Format: Requirement 'A renamed requirement states the heading it replaced' (about 430 words, 10 scenarios): the six conditions under 'The following SHALL make a document invalid:' are a <ul>. Keep the list, with a <p> inside each <li> so that every condition stays one of the requirement's statements (projection.md section 4.1 projects statements from p elements only). Paragraph 2 and list items 2 and 3 together state, for each change state, whether a renamed-from paragraph may appear: added is invalid (no previous heading), modified is valid (renamed and rewritten), unchanged is valid (renamed only), and removed is invalid (a withdrawn requirement is not also renamed). Add that as a 4-row table after the list, as a reading aid. Cells without a <p> project nothing (projection.md sections 4.1 and 8.2), so the table adds no statement. Keep every paragraph, because each carries the reason for its rule. The hard wraps at source lines 61 to 99 are the source's line structure and carry no meaning.

    Format: Headings this specification cites in its own text: 'Every semantic unit has a stable unique identifier' (in the rename requirement), the scenario 'Reference to a removed requirement' (in 'Cross-references address units by identifier'), and 'The element contract is published as a machine-readable schema' and 'A task declares completion state' (in 'A partial verification states what it did not check').     Format: Requirement 'Cross-references address units by identifier' (about 530 words, 13 scenarios): the numbered list 1 to 3 is an order of precedence, in which the first place that declares the identifier wins. The paragraph 'A change's documents are … Nothing else is reachable …', read together with items 2 and 3, is really a reachability table, so add one after it. Rows: a change's proposal, design, or tasks; a change's specification; an accepted specification; a runbook's document, a file beneath a change's evidence, or a document outside any project. Columns: the document itself, its change's specification, every accepted specification. Keep the paragraph as the statement. Its three bold sentences become <strong>.     Does: Sets the bar every staged document must clear before promotion: it decides which faults are fatal and cannot be downgraded (broken structure, references to nothing, remote or executable content, asset references that disagree with the stored bytes, change markup outside its one permitted place), which are only advisory (review findings, and a requirement no verification names, whatever outcome that verification records), and it confines the one project-level rule, duplicate asset bytes, to the stores inside `htmlspec/`. Its changes from 2026-10-02 to 2026-10-08 settle where a reference may resolve from inside a change and how an unreadable target is reported, and make a modified requirement or scenario in a change's specification the only place `ins` and `del` are legal, which is both where the migration must put its marks and why every quotation of markup in these two documents must stay escaped.

    Format: QUOTED MARKUP, requirement 'Change markup in or around a semantic unit is rejected' (1,825 words, 16 scenarios, the longest requirement in either specification). Four scenarios quote markup: 'A deleted phrase and an inserted word in one statement' quotes a whole statement, `The spellings are fixed: <code>list</code>, ... and <del>nothing else</del><ins><code>store</code></ins> SHALL name them.`; 'A change element that is itself a unit' quotes `<del class="decision">`; 'A word inserted into a modified requirement' quotes `… <code>list</code>, <code>status</code>, <ins><code>sync</code>, </ins><code>instructions</code>, and <code>store</code> name the operations OpenSpec also provides.`; and 'A word and a paragraph deleted from a modified requirement' quotes `<del>and </del>`. Escape each whole quotation as one text run inside <code>, with no live inner <code>. Here a slip changes the model as well as the look. A live `<del class="decision">` would project a decision unit inside a scenario (projection section 8.6.1), and a live ins or del in this accepted specification is rejected by the rule this requirement states.

    Format: Same requirement: 'The permission SHALL NOT extend to any of the following' introduces five bulleted exclusions, and they are its normative core. Keep them as a list with a <p> inside each <li>, so each exclusion stays one of the requirement's statements (projection sections 4.1 and 8.1). Do not make them a table, because table cells project into no field. Do not draw the permission as a decision flow either. The conditions are conjunctive, and a flow would fix which failing condition the diagnostic names first, which 'It SHALL also say why the markup is not permitted where it sits' does not decide. Keep the paragraph that names the seven places without the permission as prose, because the scenario 'The same markup outside a change's specification' already enumerates them. Keep the three bold lead sentences as <strong>, and write `ins`, `del`, `s`, `strike`, and `renamed-from` as <code> names. The quoted phrases "these words are new" and "these words were deleted" stay quotations.

    Format: Requirement 'An asset reference must match the bytes it names' (743 words, 9 scenarios): paragraphs 2 to 4 are a three-way case split written as prose. With a store found above the document, references are resolved and checked. With no store and a reference that ascends, the reference is reported. With no store and a reference that does not ascend, nothing is reported. Add a three-row table (condition, outcome, why) after those paragraphs, and put paragraph 4's reason in the last column: a fixture names a store that never existed, while an ascending reference names the store the document was generated against. Keep the paragraphs, because cells project into no field. Keep paragraph 5 (a document cannot exempt itself) and paragraph 6 (an error, not reducible) as prose.

    Format: Requirement 'A project must not store one asset's bytes more than once' (modified by 2026-09-28-confine-the-asset-check-to-the-project): from the bold sentence onward, four paragraphs partition stores three ways. A store within `htmlspec/` is compared with the project's other stores. A store outside it, while a project is in view, is checked on its own and never compared. With no project in view, every store is checked on its own. Add a three-row table (where the store is, what it is compared with, how the report names it). Keep the bold sentence as the passage's lead in <strong>, keep every paragraph, and keep the argument that a comparison reaching past `htmlspec/` changes the rule's subject to the repository as prose.

The order of places is stated in document-schema's 'Cross-references address units by identifier', so a table here would show only half of the resolution. The quoted diagnostic "No unit in the document declares that identifier" is a message, so keep it as a quotation. The cross-document citation of document-schema's heading stays quoted text. Keep both bold lead sentences as <strong>. `data-refs`, `req-x`, and `req-y` are <code> text only. They are never live attributes and never #req- links, which would dangle.

    Does: Governs a project's existence and, more than its name admits, its version history. It fixes the `htmlspec/` root with four places and one asset store, the declaration, and every property of the installed agent instructions. It also holds the archival gate that reads each archived change's recorded VERSION (never a directory name) and each published runbook's snapshot, which is why a migration must carry every VERSION file unchanged and set the declaration to the greatest one.

    Format: The title line `# project-bootstrap Specification` and the Purpose `TBD - created by archiving change project-bootstrap-cli. Update Purpose after archive.` were both written by `openspec archive`, not by an author. The other two specifications carry neither. The title becomes the document's subject. For the Purpose, see specification_notes.

    Format: Requirement 'Archival checks the versions of runbooks it publishes' (510 words, 7 scenarios): paragraph 2 is six rules in six consecutive sentences with no connective. No prior snapshot means the version must be greater than `0.0.0`. Changed canonical documents need a strictly greater version. An unchanged runbook may keep its version, or advance it with a matching changelog entry. A downgrade, a version reused for different content, or a missing version or changelog heading refuses archival. A malformed prior snapshot is reported and never treated as absent. A new or edited run record needs no increment. This is a decision table the prose compressed: make it a six-row table (runbook state against its last snapshot, what archival requires). Keep paragraph 1 (compare against the latest snapshot, ordered by recorded project versions), paragraph 3 (publication is transactional; readiness-only writes nothing), and paragraph 4 (identity is the directory name; renames, deletions, the receiving machine) as prose.

    Format: Requirement 'Tool selection is offered interactively and available without a terminal' (683 words, 10 scenarios): paragraphs 1 to 4 and 6 are a case split on how the operation was invoked. With a selection argument, it installs exactly those tools, `none` included, and does not prompt. With a terminal and no argument, it prompts with detected tools preselected, or every tool when nothing is detected. An empty confirmation at the prompt is refused and asked again, naming the no-tool argument. With no terminal, or when structured output is requested, it does not prompt and proceeds with the detected tools. Make it a four-row table (invocation, prompts, what is preselected or installed, why), carrying each paragraph's reason in the last column. Keep paragraph 5, the argument that the asymmetry between an argument and an empty confirmation is the requirement, and paragraph 7 (detection by former paths) as prose.

    Format: Requirement 'Bootstrapping installs agent instructions for the tools a project uses' (1,602 words, 15 paragraphs, 18 scenarios) is the largest in the three specifications. Five changes appended obligations to it: per-tool delivery, lifecycle coverage and order, no absent command, version stamping, argument declaration and delivery, loadable names, names that are not invocations, and one name per tool. Keep it as one requirement with its one identifier. document-schema's 'A requirement contains a title and normative statement' allows exactly one heading at the requirement's level, and splitting it would mint identifiers and obligations the accepted contract does not hold. Its scenarios already follow the paragraphs' order, so keep both in source order. The delivery kinds stay abstract (the requirement makes the tool set data, not contract), so do not add a per-tool table. That table is evidence (seven-workflow-install-2026-08-18.md).

    Format: Requirement 'Archival requires the project version to advance' (861 words, 10 scenarios): the outcomes are advanced, not moved, went backwards, unorderable, no declaration, and first archival, and each is already its own scenario. A table would restate the scenarios. The last three paragraphs argue the division of labour and why the reservation is stated on the act rather than the command. They are reasoning, not a sequence, so keep as is.

    Format: Requirement 'A project has a declared root holding one asset store' (499 words): names the four places in one sentence, then gives three bold-led argument paragraphs. Keep the paragraph order exactly. 'This sentence is not declared closed' and 'covered by that sentence' refer back to their sentences by position, and reordering would detach them.

    Format: The remaining requirements ('A project declares its name, version, and expected toolchain', 'Commands resolve the project from any directory beneath it', 'Bootstrapping is repeatable without loss', 'Instructions installed in a shared file are confined to a marked region', 'Bootstrapping ends by naming the command to run next', 'A declined or interrupted operation is distinguishable from a failure', 'The release suite checks published runbook version history') are short argued prose.     Format: Capability names appear in code spans inside statements (`runbook-authority`, `toolchain-packaging`, `project-migration`). They could become relative links to `../<capability>/spec.html`.     Does: Binds this migration and any other. The program enumerates and gates, the agent reads and decides, and the plan must show, entity by entity, which destination value each source distinction became, or that the destination has none yet and which change would add one. It is the standard a reviewer holds both the plan and the staged tree against. It also rules out, by name, the first attempt's workarounds: a note in place of a deviation, passed in place of partial, and a risk whose response defaulted to mitigated.

  • openspec/specs/runbook-execution/spec.md

    Does: Says what a run of a runbook leaves behind, and what that record is not. A run leaves one record beneath the runbook, in a place the first record creates. The record carries a whole copy of the procedure and copies of the requirements it attests to, and it stays editable while the run resumes. It is never a change and never contract. Its conformance check names the run and each requirement nothing in the record attests to. That check is evaluated only where a runbook and its runs are both in view, cannot fail validation even under the strictest setting, and stays silent for a runbook nobody has run and for a recorded failure.

  • openspec/specs/toolchain-packaging/spec.md

    Does: Fixes what the `htmlspec` program is called and how it answers, and holds the program's half of every workflow. That covers OpenSpec's command and selector spellings (each now with a request-verb second spelling), exit codes, and JSON output. It covers the archival gate, which refuses on the contract and asks about the work. It covers the one comparison of identifiers, headings, and normalized text that archival, `sync`, and `show --diff` share, none of which ever writes an accepted specification. It also carries the check suite's sandbox rules, this repository's own release record, the listing's task-state and deviation counts, store registration, and runbook preflight. Its 2026-08-10 Purpose mentions none of these.

    Format: Whole document: 25 requirements and 126 statements (124 paragraphs plus the three list items in 'The command surface reports whether a change reached the accepted contract'). It has 170 scenarios. Each has exactly one WHEN and one THEN, 69 have a GIVEN, and none has an AND. The scenarios map to the scenario description list with no irregular case.

    Format: The rule that governs every other note here: keep each source statement paragraph as exactly one <p>, in source order, and never split one into a list or merge two. 'The command surface reports whether a change reached the accepted contract' compares a requirement's statements 'in order, as one sequence of paragraphs'. 'The command surface shows a modified requirement beside the accepted one' pairs them paragraph by paragraph. The next change that modifies any of these requirements restates it from this text and is compared against it. A table recommended below is a presentational supplement placed after the statements, with no <p> in any cell. projection.md 4.1 takes statements only from paragraphs, so a cell holding a <p> would add a statement to the model and a cell without one adds none.

    Format: Requirement 'The command surface reports whether a change reached the accepted contract', paragraph 5: the three bullets (added or modified; removed; unchanged) are statements, not illustration. Each <li> must hold its text in a <p>, or the three judgements that are the core of `sync` drop out of the model (projection.md 4.1). Carry each bullet's bold opening sentence as <strong>.

    Format: Same requirement (2,673 words, 14 statements, 24 scenarios): the judgement by declared state is spread over the three bullets and the two rename paragraphs. After the statements, add a table with columns: the change's mark on the requirement | compared by | reached when | otherwise reported as. Row 1: `added` or `modified`, or `unchanged` holding a scenario marked `added`, `modified`, or `removed` | the identifier, then content: statements in order, and scenarios as a collection less those marked `removed`, with no further accepted scenario | an accepted specification holds the identifier with that content | identifier held with other content: content not taken; identifier not held: absent, and not also content. Row 2: `removed` | the identifier | no accepted specification holds it | still held: removal not taken, and never absent. Row 3: `unchanged` with no changed scenario | the identifier alone | the identifier is held | not held: absent. Row 4: any of these carrying `renamed-from`, with its identifier held | the heading names as well, after whitespace normalization | the headings agree | headings differ: untaken rename. A renamed requirement whose identifier is not held is absent only. The source states every cell. Keep as prose the paragraphs on what counts as content, on reporting where content differs (first differing paragraph, scenario identifiers, no text), on findings not being errors, and on refusal.

    Format: Requirement 'Exit codes distinguish outcomes': keep as prose, with no numbers. Numbers appear only in 'The command surface checks a runbook's machine prerequisites' and in crates/htmlspec-cli/src/exit.rs. Importing them here would add obligations this requirement does not state.

    Format: Requirements 'Output is available in human and machine forms', 'Formatting can check without writing', 'The toolchain builds reproducibly from pinned inputs', 'A development environment is provided', and 'The program is distributable as a standalone artifact': short, and already the right shape. Keep as is.

    Format: Requirement 'Project checks are runnable as one command': four constraints on every stage, each a paragraph carrying its own reason. A stage reads the working tree and not history. Every file it reads is admitted by the source filter and tracked. It passes or fails, because there is no advisory level. Its name is distinct. The reasons are the content. Keep as prose.

    Format: Requirement 'Archival produces the specification and updates the accepted contract': keep as prose. Do not draw its first sentence (produce, validate, then apply) as a sequence diagram. 'Then applies its contract changes' is in tension with 'Archival assesses the merge and never performs it' (see open_questions), and a diagram would make the disputed step look settled.

    Format: Requirement 'The command surface names its operations as OpenSpec names them' (1,788 words, 12 paragraphs, 23 scenarios). Its identifier is `req-a-single-command-exposes-validate-format-and-init`, from the rename chain (see specification_notes), so the identifier no longer matches the heading. That is what the contract requires: artifact-kinds' 'A rename reaches the accepted contract as a new heading on the same identifier' forbids a `renamed-from` paragraph in the accepted specification. Do not add one, and do not re-derive the identifier.

    Format: Same requirement, paragraph 3 ('The spellings are therefore fixed…'): keep as prose. The first attempt proposed a spelling and role table. This requirement pairs a spelling with a role in its own words only for `list`, `status`, `instructions`, `store`, `show`, the five selectors, `validate`, and `format`. It never pairs `init`, `new`, `archive`, `sync`, or `assets` with a role, so the table would either leave half its rows blank or borrow roles from other requirements. The three sentences already sort the spellings into OpenSpec's subcommands, this project's subcommands, and selectors.

    Format: Same requirement, paragraph 5 (request verbs, about 230 words in one paragraph): five verb definitions and twenty spellings grouped by verb, which is a table compressed into prose. Keep the paragraph whole as the statement. After it, add a five-row table with columns: verb | what the requirement says it means | the spellings it fixes. `get`: an operation that never writes | `get validity`, `get list`, `get status`, `get sync`, `get show`, `get assets`, `get preflight`, `get instructions`, `get registrations`, `get survey`. `post`: creates something that was not there | `post change`, `post document`, `post registration`, `post run`, `post promotion`. `put`: creates or replaces a whole thing and, run again, leaves it as one run did | `put project`, `put format`. `patch`: changes something that exists | `patch archive`. `delete`: removes something | `delete registration`. Pair a verb spelling with its OpenSpec spelling only where the requirement does: `get validity` with `validate` in the scenario, and `put format --check` with `format --check`. The full pairing is the table in the 2026-10-12 change's design decision 3, which is non-normative. Do not import it.

    Format: Same requirement: carry the three bold-led sentences as <strong>, and paragraph 4's italic phrase ('an operation that enumerates a project's active changes') as <em>. The scenarios 'Initializing a proposal', 'Initializing a specification', and 'Initializing a change' describe refusing the withdrawn spelling, and their GIVEN says so. Keep the headings as written.

    Format: Markup quoted in code spans: the angle-bracket placeholders `<runbook>`, `<record>`, and `<change>`. They appear in 'The command surface checks a runbook's machine prerequisites' (`htmlspec preflight <runbook>`, `htmlspec run <runbook> --as <record>`, `htmlspec run <runbook> --check`, and the scenario 'Reviewing existing records'). They also appear in 'The command surface shows a modified requirement beside the accepted one' (`htmlspec show <change> --diff`, `htmlspec show <change>`, and the scenarios 'A one-word modification' and 'Showing a change without a view'). Write each as &lt;runbook&gt; inside <code>. Written raw, the HTML parser makes an element, and the placeholder text silently disappears from the command.

    Format: Element names quoted in code spans: `ins` and `del`, in the 'show' paragraph 'Marks an author wrote SHALL be shown as written…' and in the scenarios 'The author's marks account for the difference' (both) and 'The author's marks leave part of the difference unmarked' (`ins`). Keep each as <code>ins</code> or <code>del</code>, never a live element. Live change markup in an accepted specification is rejected by document-validation's 'Change markup in or around a semantic unit is rejected', and a live del would also remove its words from the statement (projection.md 8.6.1). `renamed-from`, `hx-`, and the state names (`added`, `modified`, `removed`, `unchanged`, `done`, `todo`, `in-progress`, `dropped`) likewise stay <code>.

Never wrap one in href="#req-x": a same-document fragment link inside a unit projects a reference (projection.md 5.2), these identifiers resolve to nothing, and the document would be invalid.

    Format: Requirement 'An operation over a directory collects documents and not a change's evidence': walked and named paths form a small matrix. No path or a directory, within a project: every .html file beneath it except beneath a change's evidence | the same exclusion. A named file that is not a record: that file | that file.     Format: Requirement 'Archival refuses on the contract and asks about the work': two classes of condition stated as list-sentences. After the statements, add a table with columns: condition | archival's response | concerns | what the report names. Refuse, with no offer, on the contract: the declared version does not advance; there is no specification artifact; the artifact declares another kind; validating it reports an error. For these four the requirement states no report content, so leave the last cell empty. Report and offer to proceed, on the work: incomplete tasks (the count); a requirement the change adds, modifies, or carries forward that appears in no accepted specification (each identifier); a rename, a requirement's content, or a removal the accepted specifications have not taken (each requirement). Last row: a requirement the change marks `removed` that no accepted specification holds is not reported (nothing). Keep the reason sentences and the bold paragraph as prose.

2026-08-10-html-spec

Records version 0.1.0. The project's founding change. Before it, `openspec/specs/` was empty and the project was an argument in a README. It established the 0.1.0 document contract (seven semantic units, identifiers, change states, a JSON Schema plus a normative HTML-to-model projection plus conformance fixtures) and the Rust/Nix `htmlspec` toolchain that validates, formats and initializes documents, across five new capabilities. It was ordered to de-risk its bets before hardening: a typify spike, a parse-error spike, and hand-authored dogfooding of the draft vocabulary came first. Its eight evidence files record where those bets came out differently from the design's predictions: typify's `const` loss, zero benign parse recoveries, 126 bad Vega-Lite refs rather than 294, and diff locality belonging to line structure. They also record two validator defects and one template defect found late, and a print check that was never performed. Its `documents/deterministic-formatting.html` is the task 9.1 acceptance artifact. It is already in the destination format, but it was edited twice after archival and its two stylesheet references no longer resolve.

Collapsed specification. One group per capability, each opened by its Purpose paragraph, in the proposal's 'New Capabilities' order: document-schema, document-template, deterministic-formatting, document-validation, toolchain-packaging. That order is authored and runs from the contract outward to its tooling. The alphabetical order is only the filesystem's. There are 47 requirements (12 + 8 + 7 + 12 + 8) and 138 scenarios, all under `## ADDED Requirements`, so every one is `data-change="added"`. Several cross-capability pairs state a property in one capability and its enforcement in another: 'Cross-references address units by identifier' ↔ 'Cross-references must resolve'; 'A document is self-contained and offline' ↔ 'Remote and hidden network dependencies are rejected'; 'Core content is readable without JavaScript' ↔ 'No-JavaScript readability is enforced'; 'Formatting can be checked without writing' ↔ 'Formatting can check without writing'. Keep each in its capability group, because that is how the accepted specifications hold them. Cross-links between the pairs would be text the source does not contain, so they owe a reason if added.

Purpose statements. All five deltas carry an author-written `## Purpose`, not a placeholder. The document-schema Purpose is byte-identical to the accepted spec's. deterministic-formatting: canonical serialization so rich HTML yields small, meaningful Git diffs and two agents do not fight over formatting. document-schema: the normative HTML element contract for the seven semantic units, so agents address units and humans read a document rather than a data format. document-template: the canonical page (structure, visual system, print behaviour, pinned offline runtime), legible in a browser, on paper and without scripting. document-validation: the structural and safety rules and the diagnostics, so a document is machine-editable and safe to open. toolchain-packaging: the command-line surface and reproducible packaging, so everyone including CI runs the same toolchain.

Change subject. Yes. No delta says what the change as a whole did, and each Purpose describes only its own capability. A reader of specification.html alone could not tell that this change founded the project. It needs a short statement drawn from the proposal's 'Why' and 'Modified Capabilities: None': this is the project's first change, with no accepted specification before it, and it established the 0.1.0 document contract and the toolchain that validates, formats and initializes documents, across five new capabilities.

Built differs from stated. (1) document-validation 'Violations are classified by severity', scenario 'Warnings can be made fatal': as built, strict mode promotes every warning except `review/*` (`Namespace::is_promotable`). The delta states the promotion without exception (evidence/browser-verification.md defect 2; evidence/self-conformance.md finding 2). (2) document-validation 'Visualization specifications are validated', scenario 'Invalid diagram source' ('cannot be parsed by the diagram library → validation fails'): as built, Mermaid is checked only for being non-empty and having a recognized leading keyword, with a diagnostic note saying validation is shallow (design, 'Visualization sources…' and its Mermaid risk; task 4.14). A grammatically invalid diagram with a valid keyword passes. (3) document-validation 'Markup must be deterministically parseable', scenario 'Improperly nested elements → reports the location', and 'Diagnostics are actionable…' ('the location within the document'): as built, parse diagnostics name the document and the message but cannot name a line or offset (evidence/parse-errors.md, 'Gaps', limit 2). (4) document-validation 'Permitted parser recoveries are enumerated and pinned': as built, the permitted set is empty and every recovery is fatal, with 16 `parse/*` codes and a fatal catch-all `parse/unmapped-recovery`. That is consistent with the delta, but the built fact is narrower than the wording (evidence/parse-errors.md). (5) document-validation 'An upstream edit marks dependents for review…': 'changes materially' is built as 'the referenced unit declares `data-change` added or modified'. Reconciliation means returning that unit to `unchanged`, and a second rule `review/stale-verification` exists (`crates/htmlspec-validate/src/rules/review.rs` at commit 6956324; the diagnostic text in evidence/self-conformance.md). (6) document-template 'Documents share one pinned runtime', scenario 'Shared assets' ('each library appears once in the project'): as built, `init` established assets beside each document. This change's own converted document shipped with an eight-file duplicate in `documents/assets/` at archival (commit 6956324). The later change 2026-08-13-content-address-runtime-assets fixed it, and the CHANGELOG 0.1.0 entry says so. (7) deterministic-formatting 'Formatting preserves meaning', scenario 'Formatting an invalid document' (either/or): as built, the formatter refuses only markup that needs parser recovery and formats every other document, including invalid ones (task 5.5; documents/deterministic-formatting.html `decision-refuse-ambiguous`). (8) document-schema: the built projection adds explicit `data-field` (statement, note, reason, rationale, mitigation, method), a document-level `summary` from the header, and optional `figure-` identifiers that links may target (evidence/vocabulary-dogfood.md revisions table). No delta names these, and the identifier requirement's prefix list omits `figure-`. The built converted document also has decisions carrying `data-refs`, while 'Cross-references address units by identifier' lists only task, verification, evidence and risk as referencing units. That is not forbidden by the wording, but it is wider than the list. Items 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 are where a migrated specification that records what was built would read differently from the delta. The coordinator should decide how far 'the implemented result SHALL be what the migrated specification records' reaches into rewording 0.1.0 obligations.

Evidence and verification units. The change does record verification that could be cited, so omission is not automatic here. Records in the slice: evidence/browser-verification.md (offline, no-JavaScript and sibling-render guarantees verified in Firefox, with print, Chromium/WebKit and colour-vision explicitly not verified); evidence/self-conformance.md (strict validation results for four documents; narrow-width check); evidence/parse-errors.md, evidence/vega-lite-schema.md, evidence/typify-spike.md and evidence/diff-locality.md (measurements behind specific requirements); and documents/deterministic-formatting.html, whose three `verification` units (`verify-idempotence`, `verify-no-churn`, `verify-check-mode`, each `data-outcome="passed"` with a test-file method) and three `evidence` units are this change's own authored record for five of deterministic-formatting's seven requirements. Nothing in the slice verifies 'Formatting preserves meaning' or 'Generated content is ordered deterministically', and the installed validator flags both as unverified. Whether evidence and verification units in specification.html may be written from these records or must be omitted is an open question. project-migration's 'A change's delta specifications collapse…' forbids deriving them 'from a source document that was not a record of them', and these are records. Where cited, `documents/deterministic-formatting.html` is not an evidence file, and whether it is carried or preserved decides what a link to it resolves to.

Decided. Decision 2 (Scenario identifiers that collide): the two 'Reference to a removed requirement' scenarios are each derived from their requirement's heading followed by their own, recorded as scenario: notes. The rule is the migration's, since the contract is silent on scenario identifiers. The reader asked: Scenario identifier collision in the collapsed specification: document-schema ('Cross-references address units by identifier') and document-validation ('Cross-references must resolve') each hold a scenario headed 'Reference to a removed requirement'. Both derive `scenario-reference-to-a-removed-requirement` inside one specification.html. project-migration's 'Identifiers are derived once…' speaks only of requirement identifiers and forbids suffixing for requirements. The contract says nothing on how scenario identifiers are derived or on resolving a scenario collision. No requirement-heading collision exists across the five deltas when full headings are slugified.

Decided. Convention 8 (The hand-converted documents cross as they are today): the current bytes are carried into evidence/documents/deterministic-formatting.html, where promotion's checks do not reach (project-migration's "Evidence crosses unchanged"), so its unresolved references hold nothing back. The reader asked: documents/deterministic-formatting.html: which bytes are preserved (the archived 6956324 version with `htmlspec-status` and a sibling asset copy, or the current version edited by 86c33f4 and 9c3a3c7), and where it sits (the change's `evidence/` or `documents/`). No requirement decides either. Its current stylesheet references do not resolve, and its script references resolve only against the repository-root `assets/`.

Decided. Decision 1 (Creation dates), as amended: the file is carried, not dropped, so the date crosses inside evidence/.openspec.yaml. The project records no creation date, so it is neither mapped nor open. The reader asked: .openspec.yaml carries the only record of the change's start date (`created: 2026-08-04`). Dropping the file drops that date.

Decided. Convention 3 (Source paths stay as text, and links go to the migrated counterpart): the carried evidence keeps its paths untouched, and the converted proposal, design, and tasks keep the citation text and link the migrated counterpart, here the carried evidence file. The reader asked: The evidence files, carried byte-identical, cite pre-archive and repository paths (`openspec/changes/html-spec/…`, `crates/…`, `fixtures/…`, `assets/vendor.lock.json`). Those will not resolve from the migrated change, and cannot be fixed without rewriting a record. Links from the converted proposal, design and tasks should target the carried evidence files instead.
